strengths: Timely and well-motivated research question: whether traditional code complexity metrics (CC, HC, MI, CoC) reflect LLM-perceived difficulty is underexplored and practically relevant as LLMs become central to code tasks.

The preliminary empirical study (Section 2), using partial correlation controlling for code length, provides a clean and convincing demonstration that classical metrics largely lose predictive power once length is controlled for — a useful negative result in its own right.

The proposed LM-CC construction (entropy-guided semantic segmentation + hierarchical compositional/branching decomposition) is a conceptually interesting and reasonably original way to operationalize 'model-perceived' difficulty, going beyond simple perplexity aggregation.

The paper supplies an extensive theoretical appendix (assumptions, entropy-accumulation theorem, separation proposition from cyclomatic complexity, orthogonality-to-length proposition) that at least qualitatively motivates why hierarchical/branching structure should matter more than flat decision-point counts.

The causal intervention experiment (semantics-preserving rewriting to reduce LM-CC while holding cyclomatic complexity fixed) is a thoughtful attempt to move beyond correlation to a controlled causal test, and the paper discusses several plausible downstream applications (benchmark stratification, curriculum learning, adaptive reasoning) that illustrate potential significance.
weaknesses: Very small and narrow evaluation base: only 3 tasks from 2 datasets (271, 535, 162 problems), evaluated with a single LLM (DeepSeek-V3) for performance and a single, different model (CodeLlama-7B) for entropy computation — this mismatch undermines the claim that LM-CC reflects 'the' LLM's perceived difficulty, and the lack of cross-model validation limits generalizability of a metric explicitly framed as model-centric.

The feature-selection procedure (Section 3.3) and the weighting factor α (Section 4.3) are both tuned using partial correlation with the same three task datasets subsequently used to report LM-CC's correlation and causal-intervention results; there is no held-out validation split, so the reported strong correlations (r up to 0.97) are potentially inflated by in-sample tuning rather than reflecting genuine generalizable signal.

The subgroup-based correlation methodology (binning into ~9-11 groups, using median features/mean scores, then reporting the largest-magnitude statistically significant result across group counts) is a questionable practice that can substantially inflate reported correlation coefficients and constitutes a form of researcher degrees of freedom that is not adequately justified or stress-tested (e.g., no sensitivity analysis showing results are robust to binning choices).

The causal intervention experiment has confounds: rewritten samples are selected post-hoc specifically because they achieved lower LM-CC while passing tests and holding CC fixed, which could correlate with other unmeasured quality improvements introduced by the rewriting LLM (readability, variable naming, etc.) that are not captured by the theoretical mechanism claimed; there is no control condition (e.g., random semantics-preserving rewrites that do not reduce LM-CC) to isolate the causal effect. The execution-reasoning gain (97.8%→98.3%, n=60) is also very small and could plausibly be noise.

The theoretical justification (Section 3.5, Appendix B) rests on assumptions (depth-dependent degradation, branching uncertainty) that are asserted as 'empirically grounded' via loosely related literature (lost-in-the-middle, attention sinks) rather than being directly validated on code entropy data in this paper; the formal propositions (e.g., Θ(n) vs Θ(n²) separation) are illustrative constructions rather than general guarantees, and the overall derivation reads as post-hoc formalization of an already-observed empirical pattern.

Key implementation choices (entropy threshold τ=0.67, use of CodeLlama-7B for entropy, α=0.8) are justified by appeal to a single prior work on RL token selection (Wang et al., 2025b) that is not directly about code complexity segmentation, and no ablation is shown for the choice of entropy-computing model itself.

Missing simpler baselines: the paper does not compare LM-CC against simpler LLM-uncertainty-based proxies (e.g., raw total/average token entropy or perplexity without hierarchical decomposition) to demonstrate that the hierarchical/branching decomposition specifically adds value beyond aggregate model uncertainty.

strengths: The core research question—whether classical software engineering complexity metrics (CC, Halstead, MI, Cognitive Complexity) actually track LLM-perceived difficulty—is timely and underexplored, and the motivating example in Figure 1 is compelling.

The paper goes beyond correlation and attempts a causal intervention (semantics-preserving rewriting that lowers LM-CC while holding CC fixed), which is a methodologically interesting idea for establishing practical utility rather than relying solely on correlational evidence.

The hierarchical semantic decomposition combining entropy-based and syntactic boundaries is a reasonable and intuitive operationalization of 'nonlinearity' in code, and the paper attempts a formal theoretical account (entropy accumulation with depth/branching) to justify the design.
Presentation is generally clear, with good use of figures (Fig. 1-3) and a logically structured narrative from empirical motivation to metric design to validation.
weaknesses: The headline correlation numbers (Spearman r from -0.92 to -0.97) are computed on only ~9-11 group-level data points (binning hundreds of samples into ~10 groups and correlating medians/means). Correlating across such a tiny number of points is highly susceptible to producing spuriously extreme correlation coefficients, and the protocol explicitly reports 'the statistically significant result with the largest absolute correlation magnitude' across group counts 9-11 — this is a form of selective reporting/multiple comparisons that inflates apparent effect sizes and undermines the central soundness claim that LM-CC 'correlates far better' than traditional metrics.

Sample sizes are very small throughout: 271 (program repair), 535 (translation), 162 (execution reasoning) problems total, shrinking further to 58/99/60 samples after filtering for the causal rewriting experiment. These numbers are too small to support the strong, generalized claims made about 'LLM-perceived difficulty' as a general phenomenon.

All experiments rely on a single LLM family (DeepSeek-V3/V3.2) for task performance and rewriting, while entropy for LM-CC is computed with a separate, much smaller model (CodeLlama-7B). This cross-model inconsistency is never ablated — it is unclear whether LM-CC reflects genuine 'LLM-perceived' difficulty in general or is an artifact specific to CodeLlama-7B's entropy profile combined with DeepSeek's behavior. No results are shown with other model families, so claims about LLMs broadly are not well supported.

The causal rewriting experiment is confounded by its selection procedure: candidates are explicitly chosen (best-of-10 generations) to satisfy strict post-hoc filters (CC unchanged, LM-CC strictly reduced, passes/fails tests as required), which is close to directly optimizing for the metric under test. This creates a risk of tautological validation rather than an independent causal demonstration, and the reported gains are modest and based on small filtered subsets (e.g., 0.51% relative gain on execution reasoning from only 60 samples), raising doubts about practical significance and statistical robustness of the improvements.

The theoretical section (Theorem 3.3, Corollary 3.4, Proposition B.1-B.3) is largely a formalization of assumptions that are themselves unverified free parameters (δ, γ, d*), and the 'proofs' mostly restate the assumptions as inequalities rather than deriving non-trivial consequences; this gives an appearance of rigor without adding real explanatory power or being empirically calibrated.

Benchmarks are restricted to short, competitive-programming-style Python snippets (xCodeEval, HumanEval); there is no evaluation on realistic, larger-scale, multi-file, or object-oriented software, which is precisely the setting where traditional complexity metrics are most used and where LLM-perceived complexity would be most practically relevant — this substantially limits the significance and external validity of the findings.

Key methodological choices (entropy threshold τ=0.67, weighting factor α=0.8) are borrowed or tuned post hoc on the same small evaluation tasks used for the headline results, raising concerns about overfitting the metric design to the specific benchmarks rather than demonstrating a principled, transferable complexity measure.

No code or data release is mentioned, and critical implementation details (e.g., exact hierarchy construction thresholds, significance testing procedure for the 20.9%/10.2%/0.51% gains) are deferred to appendices or omitted, limiting reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored question—whether classical code complexity metrics (CC, HC, MI, CoC) actually track LLM-perceived difficulty—and provides a clear empirical demonstration that they largely do not once code length is partialled out.

The proposed LM-CC metric is conceptually well-motivated: grounding semantic unit boundaries in token-level entropy and organizing them into a compositional hierarchy that separately captures nesting depth and branching is a reasonable and relatively novel operationalization of 'model-perceived' complexity.

The evaluation goes beyond correlation: a causal intervention (semantics-preserving rewriting that lowers LM-CC while holding cyclomatic complexity fixed) is used to show that reducing the proposed metric actually improves pass@1, which is a stronger form of evidence than typical complexity-metric papers provide.

The theoretical appendix attempts to formally explain why hierarchical/branching structure, rather than raw decision-point counts, should matter for predictive entropy, and gives a constructive proof (flat vs. nested conditionals) showing CC and LM-CC can diverge sharply at fixed code length.
Feature-selection and ablation analyses (Table 2, Fig. 3) are included rather than simply asserting the final weighted formula, giving some transparency into how the metric design choices were made.
Clear writing and figures (e.g., Figure 1/2) that make the core intuition accessible.
weaknesses: All correlation results rely on a subgroup-binning procedure (collapsing each task to ~10 group-level points, median/mean aggregated) and then reporting the best result among 9–11 different binnings that reaches significance; this risks inflating and cherry-picking correlation magnitudes and is a nonstandard, somewhat opaque statistical practice for the paper's central quantitative claims (e.g., r up to 0.97).

All experiments use a single LLM (DeepSeek-V3) for task performance, while entropy for LM-CC is computed with a different, much smaller model (CodeLlama-7B). This conflates 'LLM-perceived difficulty' across two different models and raises doubts about generalization to other architectures/scales; no cross-model validation is reported.

Dataset sizes are small (271, 535, 162 problems) and shrink further after filtering for the causal rewriting experiment (58, 99, 60 samples), with gains as small as 0.51% relative improvement reported without confidence intervals, effect-size context, or details of the significance test behind the '†' markers.

The hyperparameters τ=0.67 and α=0.8 are selected using the same three tasks/datasets used for the main correlation and intervention results, creating a risk of circularity: the metric may be tuned to perform well on exactly the data used to validate it, and the α ablation shows high sensitivity for program repair, suggesting limited robustness.

The semantics-preserving rewriting used for causal validation is performed by an LLM instructed only to preserve functionality and hold cyclomatic complexity fixed; this control does not rule out other confounds introduced by LLM rewriting (e.g., more idiomatic/in-distribution style, naming conventions, variable scoping changes) that could independently affect pass@1 irrespective of the hierarchical/branching structure targeted by LM-CC.

The feature-selection step (choosing TotalCompLevel and TotalBranch as the 'most representative' features) is based on only three tasks, which is a narrow basis for generalizing the specific weighted formulation.

Limited language/task diversity: essentially Python-centric experiments (and Python-to-C translation), with no evaluation on more structurally diverse or longer real-world codebases (e.g., repository-level tasks), which limits claims about broader applicability.

The theoretical results (Theorem 3.3, Corollary 3.4) are largely restatements of the stated assumptions (additive entropy penalties) rather than derivations that independently predict the specific weighted-sum form of LM-CC; the formal results mainly justify a design choice post hoc rather than derive it.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely interesting and underexplored question: whether classical, execution-centric code complexity metrics (CC, Halstead, MI, Cognitive Complexity) actually track the difficulty LLMs experience with code, and provides a systematic length-controlled partial-correlation study across three tasks and multiple metrics showing these metrics largely fail to correlate once code length is controlled for.

The proposed LM-CC metric is conceptually well motivated (entropy-guided semantic segmentation + compositional hierarchy capturing nesting depth and branching), and the paper supplies a reasonably complete pipeline (algorithm, formal setup, worked example in Figure 2).

Fairly extensive empirical validation: correlation analysis across 4 entropy-estimation backbones, 3-4 task-performing LLMs (DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o-mini, and an additional model), and 4 tasks, plus an ablation on the decomposition strategy and the weighting factor α.

The causal intervention experiment (semantics-preserving, CC-controlled rewriting to reduce LM-CC) is a nice complement to correlational analysis and provides some evidence of practical utility beyond mere association.

Formal theoretical analysis (Proposition B.1, Theorem 3.3) offers an interpretable separation argument between LM-CC and cyclomatic complexity via a flat-vs-nested construction, which is a useful sanity check even if not deeply novel.
weaknesses: Circularity/overfitting risk in metric construction: the two constituent features (TotalCompLevel, TotalBranch) are selected because they already showed the highest significant-correlation coverage on the very same evaluation tasks/datasets (Section 3.3), and the weighting factor α=0.8 is likewise tuned via ablation on the same three core tasks used to report LM-CC's correlation strength in Table 2/Section 4.1. There is no held-out task or dataset split for feature/weight selection versus evaluation, so the reported superiority of LM-CC over its components and over traditional metrics is partly a consequence of post-hoc optimization on the test data rather than independent validation.

No comparison against a simple, non-hierarchical LLM-based baseline (e.g., mean/total token-level perplexity or entropy of the whole snippet without any hierarchical decomposition). Such a baseline is the most natural competitor to isolate whether the hierarchical/branching structure actually adds value beyond raw entropy, and its absence weakens the claim that hierarchy per se (rather than entropy signal generally) is responsible for the gains.

Sample sizes are small throughout (271 and 535 problems from xCodeEval, 162 from HumanEval, and only 58/99/60 samples in the causal rewriting experiment after filtering), and correlation is computed via subgroup binning into ~10 groups with a search over 9-11 bins reporting the most significant result, which increases the risk of researcher degrees of freedom and reduces confidence in the reported correlation magnitudes.

The threshold τ=0.67 for entropy-based boundary detection is imported from an unrelated prior work on RL token selection rather than derived or validated specifically for code segmentation; Proposition B.3 only shows that a threshold can separate bimodal entropy under idealized assumptions, not that τ=0.67 is appropriate for this setting.

The theoretical contribution (Assumptions 3.1/3.2, Theorem 3.3, Corollary 3.4) is largely a restatement of the metric definition with unspecified constants (δ, γ, d*) that are never estimated or validated empirically; it does not yield falsifiable predictions beyond what the empirical correlation study already shows, limiting its explanatory value.

The causal rewriting experiment involves generating up to n=10 candidate rewrites per sample and post-hoc filtering for those that reduce LM-CC (while holding CC fixed), which introduces a selection process that could also correlate with other confounds (e.g., general code quality/readability improvements made by the rewriting LLM) not fully disentangled from the LM-CC-specific effect; statistical significance testing procedures for the reported "significant" improvements in Table 3 are not described.

Execution reasoning gains from complexity reduction are marginal (94.1%→95.0%), and given the near-ceiling baseline and small filtered sample (n=60), the practical significance of this result is questionable despite being labeled statistically significant.

Reported per-sample computation cost for LM-CC (up to 0.7s/sample) is orders of magnitude higher than traditional metrics (sub-millisecond), which is only briefly acknowledged and could limit scalability for large-scale corpus analysis or training-time use cases despite claims of parallelizability.

Only a single primary task-performing model (DeepSeek-V3) is used for the main text results, with additional models relegated to the appendix; the main paper would benefit from more diverse and open primary experiments to strengthen generalizability claims made in the abstract.

strengths: Addresses a timely and interesting question: whether classical, human-oriented complexity metrics (cyclomatic complexity, Halstead, MI, cognitive complexity) actually track the difficulty LLMs experience on code tasks.

The initial empirical study (Section 2) showing that zero-order correlations of traditional metrics largely vanish once code length is partialled out is a useful and clearly presented negative result.

The proposed LM-CC metric is evaluated across a reasonably wide set of tasks (program repair, translation, execution reasoning, summarization), four entropy-estimation backbones, and (in the appendix) three task-performing LLMs, showing broadly consistent negative correlations.

The causal intervention experiment (semantics-preserving rewriting that lowers LM-CC while holding cyclomatic complexity fixed) is a nice attempt to move beyond correlational evidence toward a demonstration of practical utility.
The paper is generally well organized, with a clear narrative arc from empirical motivation to metric design to theoretical rationale to experiments.
weaknesses: Statistical methodology for the core correlational claims is weak: correlations are computed on ~10 group-level points obtained by binning samples into subgroups, and the paper explicitly reports 'the largest absolute correlation magnitude' across a range of bin counts (9–11) that reaches p<0.05 — this is closer to a search for a favorable configuration than a pre-registered, robust estimator, and the extremely small effective sample size (n≈10) makes claimed r values of -0.9+ far less informative than the paper implies. No confidence intervals or correction for the many (16+) correlation tests reported per table are provided.

Potential circularity/self-fulfilling design: LM-CC is built directly from token-level entropy of a language model, i.e., it is a model's own predictive uncertainty. Showing that a downstream LLM performs worse on high-entropy code is close to restating that 'code that is hard for one LM (in next-token prediction) is hard for another LM (in task performance)', which is a much weaker and more expected claim than 'a novel notion of code complexity' would suggest.

The ablation in Table 5 (syntax-only vs. entropy-only vs. full LM-CC) shows that a purely syntax-driven hierarchical decomposition (with no entropy at all) already achieves comparable or even superior correlations in several settings (e.g., -0.88 vs -0.93 for program repair, -0.99 vs -0.93 for Qwen3.5-122B program repair). This undermines the central thesis that entropy-grounded semantic segmentation is what drives the improvement over traditional metrics, since much of the gain appears attributable simply to using hierarchical depth/branching features rather than flat scalar metrics like CC.

The weighting parameter α (set to 0.8) is chosen via an ablation run on what appears to be the same evaluation tasks/datasets used to report the main results, raising concerns about implicit overfitting/data leakage rather than genuine generalization; no held-out validation protocol for α selection is described.

The causal rewriting experiment has confounds that are not adequately controlled: the rewriting model is prompted to 'improve comprehensibility/readability,' and samples are post-hoc filtered to those where LM-CC decreased and CC stayed constant. It is plausible that readability-improving rewrites by a strong LLM improve downstream pass@1 for reasons unrelated to the specific LM-CC construct (e.g., variable renaming, removing dead code, clarifying logic) — the design does not rule out that any comprehensibility-oriented rewrite, not one specifically targeting the entropy-hierarchy construct, would yield similar gains.

The theoretical section (Theorem 3.3, Corollary 3.4, Proposition B.1/B.2) rests on loosely motivated assumptions (Assumptions 3.1, 3.2) stated with unspecified constants (δ, γ, d*), and the 'proofs' largely restate the assumptions as additive bounds without empirical estimation of these constants or validation that the assumptions hold quantitatively for real code; the toy code constructions in Proposition B.1 (fully flat vs. fully nested conditionals) are somewhat artificial and may not represent realistic code complexity variation.

Dataset sizes are modest (271, 535, 162 problems) and, combined with the binning procedure, further reduce the reliability of the reported statistics; reproducibility is also limited since the source code link is left empty in the submission.
Some models cited in the appendix (e.g., 'Qwen3.5-122B') do not correspond to any publicly documented release and lack a citation entry, raising concerns about the experimental setup's verifiability.

The paper's actual technical contribution is a fairly simple weighted linear combination of two hand-crafted aggregate features (TotalBranch, TotalCompLevel) computed over a heuristically segmented hierarchy (entropy threshold + structural delimiters); despite the extensive framing, the core method is a relatively lightweight, empirically-tuned formula rather than a principled or learned model of LLM difficulty.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored question: whether classical structural complexity metrics (cyclomatic complexity, Halstead, MI, cognitive complexity) actually track the difficulty LLMs experience with code, rather than assuming this by default as prior work has largely done.

The preliminary study (Section 2) is a useful contribution in its own right: it systematically shows that zero-order correlations between traditional metrics and pass@1 largely vanish once code length is partialled out, which is a clean and informative negative result.

Broad empirical validation of LM-CC: correlations are computed across three-to-four tasks (program repair, code translation, execution reasoning, code summarization), four different entropy-estimation backbones, and three different task-performing LLMs (DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o-mini, Qwen3.5-122B) in the appendix, giving reasonable evidence of robustness and cross-model generalization.

The causal intervention experiment (Section 4.2) is a nice complement to the correlational analysis: rewriting code to reduce LM-CC while explicitly holding cyclomatic complexity fixed and requiring functional equivalence is a sensible design for isolating the effect of the proposed metric from conventional structural simplification.
Ablation studies on the decomposition strategy (entropy-only vs. syntax-only vs. combined) and the weighting parameter α provide some insight into which design choices matter.
The paper is generally clearly written, with an intuitive running example (Figure 1/2) that helps ground the abstract notion of "semantic nonlinearity."
weaknesses: The correlation analysis relies on binning ~150-500 samples into ~10 groups and computing Spearman correlation on the resulting ~10 group-level points; reporting "the statistically significant result with the largest absolute correlation magnitude" across group counts 9–11 (Appendix C) is a form of researcher-degree-of-freedom / selection procedure that can inflate apparent effect sizes and should be justified more rigorously or replaced with a pre-registered single procedure plus confidence intervals.

The theoretical derivation (Section 3.5, Appendix B) is largely a restatement of the empirical hypothesis in formal notation: Assumptions 3.1/3.2 introduce unconstrained constants (δ, γ, d*) that are never estimated or validated, and Theorem 3.3's proof is a nearly trivial additive decomposition. The "formal separation" from CC (Proposition B.1) is a constructed worst-case example rather than evidence that this asymmetry is common or predictive in practice.

The semantics-preserving rewriting experiment used to establish causality is somewhat weakly controlled: the rewriting prompt asks an LLM to "improve comprehensibility and readability" in general (not to specifically minimize LM-CC as an isolated variable), and among 10 sampled attempts only those with decreased LM-CC and unchanged CC are retained. This selection could favor generically "better" rewrites (e.g., clearer variable names, formatting) whose benefit is not uniquely attributable to reduced LM-CC, since LM-CC is computed only after removing comments/docstrings and thus may not capture all sources of readability improvement that the LLM introduces.

The final metric itself (a linear combination of just two aggregate features, TotalBranch and TotalCompLevel, with an empirically tuned α=0.8) is comparatively simple relative to the elaborate hierarchical/entropy machinery and theoretical apparatus built up to justify it; the paper would benefit from directly comparing LM-CC against simpler baselines (e.g., mean token entropy/perplexity alone, or entropy-weighted length) to show the hierarchical decomposition is necessary rather than incidental.

Hyperparameters (τ=0.67 borrowed from an unrelated RL paper, α=0.8 chosen via ablation on the same three core tasks) are calibrated on the same benchmarks used for the main evaluation; the claim of "generalization" to code summarization is only a single held-out task and does not fully address possible overfitting of these hyperparameters to the specific benchmark suite.

The repository link for reproducibility is left blank ("source code is available at:"), and full experimental details (e.g., exact prompts for program repair/translation, dataset preprocessing beyond token entropy) are only partially specified, which may hinder exact reproducibility.

The intervention experiment operates on fairly small filtered subsets (58, 99, 60 samples after top-50/60% LM-CC filtering), and improvements, while statistically marked as significant, are computed on paired subsets that already exclude "easy" cases, which may not generalize to the full benchmark distribution.
